candidates.name: Bulk Task Surgery
candidates.description: Multi-select tasks and change owner, date, or status across hundreds of rows at once.
candidates.problem: Owner, date and status change one task at a time. A two-week slip is eighty manual edits, and a departure is two hours of clicking.
candidates.counterweight: The most-mentioned item in the whole corpus, worth $31k. It's a retention and daily-satisfaction problem rather than a sales one — which is precisely why it never shows up in a lost-deal reason.

evidence.quote: When a project slips two weeks I have to open eighty tasks and change eighty due dates. One at a time.
Give me a checkbox and a change-owner button and you've saved me an afternoon a week.
Somebody left the team last month. Reassigning their work took me two hours of clicking.
Bulk edit isn't glamorous but it's the difference between the tool helping and the tool being a chore.
Every single person on my team has complained about not being able to change more than one task at a time.
I can select multiple tasks but the only thing I can do with the selection is delete them, which is terrifying.
Multi-select and bulk edit. That's it, that's the whole request.
It comes down to Slack integration was one-way notifications only and editing tasks one at a time was untenable at that volume. Everything else we could have lived with.

candidates.name: Guest Passes
candidates.description: Free, scoped external collaborators so clients and agencies participate without a paid seat.
candidates.problem: External clients and agencies need a paid seat to see anything, so teams email screenshots and approvals happen outside the tool.
candidates.counterweight: The loudest ask in the corpus by a wide margin — and a pricing decision, not just a product one. Free guest seats may cost more in seat revenue than the deals they win.

evidence.quote: Can a guest comment and approve without being able to wander into other projects?
Today we email screenshots to clients. It's 2026 and we are emailing screenshots.
Half the people on any given project don't work here. Am I buying seats for our clients?
Our agency partners live in this tool with us or the whole thing falls apart.
We need guest access. Client comes in, sees their project, sees nothing else, costs me nothing.
The approval loop is the bottleneck, and the approver is always someone outside the company.
If every external reviewer needs a full license this gets expensive fast, and my CFO will notice.

It comes down to external client collaboration would have required paying for every guest seat; no workload or capacity view to prevent over-allocating the team; and no dependency-aware timeline for the delivery plan. Everything else we could have lived with.

candidates.name: Workload Radar
candidates.description: Capacity view showing who is over-allocated across every project before the sprint starts.
candidates.problem: Nobody can see who is over-allocated across projects until they say so, and resourcing lives in a spreadsheet that's wrong the moment it's saved.
candidates.counterweight: Nineteen calls, and the fastest-rising thing in the backlog — first raised barely a year ago. Trajectory, not just volume.

evidence.quote: We're on a resourcing spreadsheet that is wrong roughly four minutes after saving, which is why I'm on this call.
If I assign one more task to someone at a hundred and twenty percent, the tool should tell me.
I want a workload view. People down one axis, weeks across the top, red where they're over.
I have no idea who is drowning until they tell me they're drowning, and by then it's late.
Show me utilisation by person, and let me drag work to someone with room.
Resourcing conversations happen in a spreadsheet that's wrong the moment I save it.
Our designers sit on six projects each. Nobody can see the total, including the designers.
Capacity planning is the reason I'm shopping. Everything else we have.

It comes down to external client collaboration would have required paying for every guest seat; no workload or capacity view to prevent over-allocating the team; no dependency-aware timeline for the delivery plan; and mobile app unusable on job sites without connectivity. candidates.name: Timeline View

candidates.problem: No dependency-aware schedule. A slipped milestone moves nothing downstream, and the exec schedule gets rebuilt by hand every week.
candidates.counterweight: Seventeen calls, but often a request on behalf of a stakeholder who will never log in. Worth asking whether the buyer wants the view or wants the slide.

evidence.quote: Can I see the critical path? When something slips I need to know immediately whether the launch date moved.
Every client kickoff starts with a schedule slide. I'm rebuilding that slide by hand every single week.
My exec team thinks in Gantt charts. I can hand them a board and they will hand it straight back.
We need a timeline view. Not a calendar, a real timeline with dependencies drawn on it.
If I move one milestone, everything after it should move too. Does it do that?
The board view is great for the team and useless for my steering committee.

candidates.name: Custom Fields
candidates.description: User-defined typed fields on tasks and projects, filterable and reportable everywhere.
candidates.problem: Intake data has nowhere to live, so teams overload tags and end up with four hundred of them and no way to report.
candidates.counterweight: Fifteen calls, and a foundation other things stand on — reporting, filtering and automation all get harder to build without it. Cheap to underrate.

evidence.quote: We tried using tags for this and ended up with four hundred tags. It's a mess.
Formula fields would be a nice-to-have, plain custom fields are the requirement.
Can I add a dropdown field and then filter the whole workspace by it?
Custom fields need to work in reporting too, otherwise what's the point of capturing them.
Our intake form has nine questions. All nine need somewhere to live on the task.
Every request has a client code and a billing type. Those need to be real fields, not text in the description.

candidates.name: Slack Two-Way
candidates.description: Bidirectional Slack sync so a thread reply lands on the task and a task update lands in channel.
candidates.problem: The integration is one-way. A reply in a Slack thread never reaches the task, so the tool and the conversation drift apart.
candidates.counterweight: Thirteen calls and $31k. Genuinely loved and genuinely not worth money — nobody has bought or refused to buy over it.

evidence.quote: It's Slack, entirely Slack, with a tool they open when someone nags them, and it works right up until it doesn't.
We'd want per-channel routing, so the design channel only hears about design work.
Notifications into a channel is the easy half. I want a reply in the thread to post back as a comment.
My team lives in Slack. If they have to leave Slack to update a task, they won't update the task.
The integration you have now is one-way and everybody ignores it.
Honestly the tool that wins here is the one that makes Slack the interface.
It comes down to Slack integration was one-way notifications only and editing tasks one at a time was untenable at that volume. Everything else we could have lived with.
Can I create a task from a Slack message? That's the moment the work actually gets named.

candidates.name: Time Tracking
candidates.description: Native time entry against tasks, with rollups per person, project, and billing period.
candidates.problem: Hours live in a second tool, so billable work goes unlogged and someone reconciles a spreadsheet every Friday.
candidates.counterweight: Asked for constantly by agencies and consultancies, and shipped by every competitor. Table stakes rather than differentiation — losing without it is more likely than winning with it.

evidence.quote: Can you start a timer on a task? That's the whole ask.
We bill clients hourly. If time doesn't live next to the task, people don't log it, and then we don't invoice it.
The finance team pulls timesheets on the second. If that's a manual export I'm the one doing it.
We need hours rolled up by project for month end. Doesn't have to be fancy.
Right now the team tracks hours in a spreadsheet and someone reconciles it every Friday. It's genuinely miserable.
I'd want to see estimated versus actual on every task, otherwise our estimates never improve.

It comes down to external client collaboration would have required paying for every guest seat; no native time tracking, forcing a second tool for billing; no dependency-aware timeline for the delivery plan; and custom fields too limited to model their intake process. Everything else we could have lived with.

candidates.name: Audit Trail
candidates.description: Immutable, exportable log of every change to a project, task, or permission.
candidates.problem: Nobody can answer “who changed this, and when”. A due date moves with no author attached, and an auditor asking for a change log gets an activity feed nobody can archive.
candidates.counterweight: Seven lost deals, but every one died at security review — late, after months of sales effort. The real cost isn't only the ARR, it's the cycle time spent reaching a gate we always fail.

evidence.quote: The tool we're on now has an audit export and that's genuinely the only reason we still pay for it.
Right now if a due date moves, nobody can tell me who moved it. That's the whole problem.
We need a full audit history. Every edit, every access change, with a timestamp and a person attached.
Internal audit does a quarterly pull. If I can't hand them a change log for the whole workspace, this doesn't get through review.
SOC 2 auditors want evidence. An activity feed in the UI isn't evidence, I need a CSV I can archive.
Our compliance team is going to ask who changed what and when. Can you export that?
Does the history go back forever, or does it roll off? Because a ninety day window is useless to us.

It comes down to no portfolio-level roll-up for leadership reporting; no SAML single sign-on, which IT treated as non-negotiable; no exportable audit history for the compliance team; and permissions too coarse to keep contractors out of internal projects. Everything else we could have lived with.

I want project-level roles, not just workspace-level. That's the gap.

candidates.problem: IT can't provision or deprovision through the company identity provider. Every user is a separate password, and a leaver keeps their access until someone remembers.
candidates.counterweight: Only nine calls mention it because it rarely survives to a second conversation — it's a qualification gate, not a feature request. A low mention count here means the opposite of low demand.

We're an Okta shop. Everything has to sign in through Okta, no exceptions.

candidates.name: Portfolio Roll-Up
candidates.description: One cross-project view of status, spend, and risk for leadership, updated without manual reporting.
candidates.problem: Leadership has no cross-project view, so the PMO spends the first two days of every month assembling a status deck by hand.
candidates.counterweight: Only seven calls, but every one came from a buyer running sixty-plus projects — the largest seat counts and the slowest churn in the pipeline.

evidence.quote: Right now it's a PMO that reports upward in slides and downward in email. Nobody's proud of it.
Leadership wants a portfolio view. Status, spend, and risk across every program in one place.
My PMO spends the first two days of every month assembling a status deck by hand. That's the thing I'm trying to kill.
I run sixty projects. I need one screen that tells me which ones are red, without opening sixty tabs.
Can I group projects into programs, and programs into a portfolio? Three levels, basically.

Everything else we could have lived with.

candidates.name: API Throughput
candidates.description: Higher API rate limits and bulk endpoints so large workspaces can sync without backing off.
candidates.problem: Rate limits are too low for a nightly warehouse sync, so integration jobs back off and an eleven-hour window isn't enough.
candidates.counterweight: Five calls and $935k — the highest revenue-per-mention in the backlog. Everyone who raises it is technical, large, and already committed to integrating.

evidence.quote: We sync everything into Snowflake nightly. At your current rate limit that job takes eleven hours.
Our integration team hit your rate limit in the trial. That's not a great sign for production.
Is there a bulk endpoint? Paginating a hundred thousand tasks at that limit is not viable.
We'd need a much higher API ceiling, and ideally webhooks so we're not polling at all.
Everything we buy has to feed the warehouse. If the API can't keep up, it doesn't get bought.

belowThreshold.name: Template Market
belowThreshold.description: Shared library of project templates teams can publish internally and pull from.
belowThreshold.problem: Every project manager sets projects up differently, so conventions live in people's heads and new starters spend their first week learning them.
belowThreshold.counterweight: $19k of lost deals makes this look trivial, but every new customer hits it in week one. It's an onboarding-time lever, and onboarding time is a leading indicator ARR can't see.

evidence.quote: We'd publish our own templates internally if you gave us somewhere to put them.
Is there a template gallery? Even a basic one would save the onboarding conversation.
New PMs spend their first week figuring out our conventions. A template would just tell them.
Every project manager sets up projects differently. I want one blessed template everyone starts from.

belowThreshold.name: Recurring Tasks
belowThreshold.description: Tasks and checklists that regenerate on a schedule without anyone remembering to clone them.
belowThreshold.problem: Repeating checklists are duplicated by hand every cycle, and someone has to remember to do it.
belowThreshold.counterweight: Four calls, no lost deals, and probably a week of work. The kind of item that never wins a vote and never stops being asked for.

evidence.quote: I'd want the recurrence to skip weekends, but that's detail.
Recurring maintenance work is maybe forty percent of what we do.
We run the same twelve-step checklist every month. Someone duplicates it by hand every month.
Can a task repeat weekly? Genuinely surprised that's not in here.

belowThreshold.name: Offline Mode
belowThreshold.description: Mobile app that keeps working on a job site with no signal and syncs when it reconnects.
belowThreshold.problem: Field crews lose signal on site and the app stalls, so work orders go back to paper and sync never happens.
belowThreshold.counterweight: Three calls, two of them lost deals. A narrow vertical requirement that is absolute when it applies and irrelevant when it doesn't.

evidence.quote: The short answer is crews on paper work orders because the app does not work in basements.
The mobile app is fine in the office, which is the one place nobody needs it.
Field techs need to update jobs offline and have it sync later. That's non-negotiable for us.

belowThreshold.name: Uptime SLA
belowThreshold.description: Contractual uptime guarantee with a public status page and incident history.
belowThreshold.problem: No contractual uptime commitment and no public status page, so procurement has nothing to review and vendor approval stalls.
belowThreshold.counterweight: Three calls, $421k. Mostly a legal and process change rather than engineering work — unusually cheap for the revenue it unblocks.

evidence.quote: Do you have a public status page? Our vendor review checks for one.
If you go down during our launch week I need to know what the remedy is, contractually.
Procurement needs a written uptime commitment. Ninety-nine point nine, in the contract.

belowThreshold.name: Dark Mode
belowThreshold.description: A dark theme across the whole product, respecting the system setting.
belowThreshold.problem: No dark theme, and the product ignores the system setting entirely.
belowThreshold.counterweight: Zero lost deals and zero revenue behind it. Nothing here argues for shipping it except that it's small, popular, and visible on the first day.

evidence.quote: Not a dealbreaker at all, but dark mode would make people happy on day one.
Is there a dark theme? Our engineers will complain, they always complain.
Half my team asked me to ask you about dark mode. So, dark mode.

belowThreshold.name: AI Standup Digest
belowThreshold.description: Generated daily summary of what moved, what stalled, and what needs a decision.
belowThreshold.problem: Nobody knows what actually moved yesterday without opening every project and reading it.
belowThreshold.counterweight: Two mentions, both unprompted asides at the end of a call. There's almost no evidence behind this one — judge it on conviction, because the corpus has nothing to say.

evidence.quote: If it could tell me each morning what actually changed yesterday, I'd read that every day.
Everyone's shipping AI summaries now. Do you have anything that writes the standup for me?
